claim: Efference copies refer to internal duplicates of movement-producing neural signals.
source: Efference copies refer to internal duplicates of movement-producing neural signals.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The primary function of efference copies is to predict, and often suppress, the sensory consequences of willed movements.
source: Their primary function is to predict, and often suppress, the sensory consequences of willed movements.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific understanding of efference copies.

claim: Efference copies have been almost exclusively investigated in the context of overt movements.
source: Efference copies have been almost exclusively investigated in the context of overt movements.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of the literature, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: The production of an inner phoneme resulted in electrophysiological suppression when the content of the inner phoneme matched the content of the audible phoneme.
source: The production of the inner phoneme resulted in electrophysiological suppression, but only if the content of the inner phoneme matched the content of the audible phoneme.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Inner speech is associated with an efference copy with detailed auditory properties.
source: These results demonstrate that inner speech – a purely mental action – is associated with an efference copy with detailed auditory properties.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing content-specific suppression.

claim: Inner speech may ultimately reflect a special type of overt speech.
source: These findings suggest that inner speech may ultimately reflect a special type of overt speech.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Self-generated sensations feel less salient than externally-generated sensations which are physically identical.
source: Sensory attenuation – also known as self-suppression – refers to the phenomenon that self-generated sensations feel less salient, and evoke a smaller neurophysiological response, than externally-generated sensations which are physically identical (Hughes et al., 2013; Cardoso-Leite et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Self-generated sensations evoke a smaller neurophysiological response than externally-generated sensations which are physically identical.
source: Sensory attenuation – also known as self-suppression – refers to the phenomenon that self-generated sensations feel less salient, and evoke a smaller neurophysiological response, than externally-generated sensations which are physically identical (Hughes et al., 2013; Cardoso-Leite et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sensory attenuation is believed to result from the action of an internal forward model.
source: Sensory attenuation is believed to result from the action of an internal forward model, or IFM (Blakemore et al., 2000a; Wolpert and Miall, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The sensory consequences of self-generated movements are predicted based on a copy of the outgoing motor command, known as an efference copy.
source: According to this account, the sensory consequences of self-generated movements are predicted based on a copy of the outgoing motor command, known as an efference copy.
evidence: This is a description of the internal forward model theory, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Predicted sensations are compared to the actual sensations resulting from the movement.
source: These predicted sensations are compared to the actual sensations resulting from the movement, and the difference between predicted and actual sensation (i.e., the sensory discrepancy – Wolpert and Miall, 1996) is sent higher up the neuronal hierarchy for further processing (Seth and Friston, 2016).
evidence: This statement describes the internal forward model mechanism and is supported by citations.

claim: In the case of a self-generated movement, the internal prediction is able to account for, and 'explain away', much of the resulting sensation.
source: In the case of a self-generated movement, the internal prediction is able to account for, and 'explain away', much of the resulting sensation, which is why self-initiated sensations typically feel less salient, and evoke a smaller neurophysiological response, than externally-initiated sensations (Blakemore et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The amplitude of the N1 component is sensitive to sound intensity, with loud sounds evoking larger N1 amplitudes than soft sounds.
source: The amplitude of this component is known to be sensitive to sound intensity; i.e., loud sounds evoke larger N1 amplitudes than soft sounds (Näätänen and Picton, 1987; Hegerl and Juckel, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Self-generated vocalizations elicit an N1 component of smaller amplitude than the N1 component elicited when passively listening to the same sounds.
source: Numerous electroencephalographic (EEG) and magnetoencephalographic (MEG) studies have found that self-generated vocalizations elicit an N1 component (M100 in the MEG) of smaller amplitude than the N1 component elicited when passively listening to the same sounds (Ford et al., 2007a; Curio et al., 2000; Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2005; Oestreich et al., 2015; Houde et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: N1-suppression suggests that self-generated sounds are processed as though they were physically softer than externally-generated sounds.
source: This phenomenon has been dubbed N1-suppression, and it suggests that self-generated sounds are processed as though they were physically softer than externally-generated sounds, reflecting the action of an IFM (Greenlee et al., 2011; Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2006).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Experimentally altering auditory feedback reduces the amount of N1-suppression.
source: The suggestion that an IFM is responsible for sensory attenuation to overt speech is bolstered by the finding that experimentally altering auditory feedback (e.g., by pitch-shifting or delaying an individual's voice, such that auditory sensations do not match the predictions of the IFM) reduces the amount of N1-suppression (Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2006; Behroozmand and Larson, 2011; Behroozmand et al., 2011; Aliu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Inner speech refers to the silent production of words in one's mind.
source: Inner speech – also known as covert speech, imagined speech, or verbal thoughts – refers to the silent production of words in one's mind (Perrone-Bertolotti et al., 2014; Alderson-Day and Fernyhough, 2015).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: Most people spend at least a quarter of their lives engaged in inner speech.
source: Inner speech is one of the most pervasive and ubiquitous of human activities; it has been estimated that most people spend at least a quarter of their lives engaged in inner speech (Heavey and Hurlburt, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Inner speech ultimately reflects a special case of overt speech in which the articulator organs do not actually move.
source: An influential account of inner speech suggests that it ultimately reflects a special case of overt speech in which the articulator organs (e.g., mouth, tongue, larynx) do not actually move; that is, inner speech is conceptualized as 'a kind of action' (Jones and Fernyhough, 2007, p.396 – see also Feinberg, 1978; Pickering and Garrod, 2013; Oppenheim and Dell, 2010).
evidence: This statement describes an influential theoretical account and is supported by citations.

claim: Inner speech activates similar brain regions to overt speech, including audition and language-related perceptual areas and supplementary motor areas.
source: Support for this idea has been provided by studies showing that inner speech activates similar brain regions to overt speech, including audition and language-related perceptual areas and supplementary motor areas, but does not typically activate primary motor cortex (Palmer et al., 2001; Zatorre et al., 1996; Aleman et al., 2005; Shuster and Lemieux, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Inner speech does not typically activate primary motor cortex.
source: Support for this idea has been provided by studies showing that inner speech activates similar brain regions to overt speech, including audition and language-related perceptual areas and supplementary motor areas, but does not typically activate primary motor cortex (Palmer et al., 2001; Zatorre et al., 1996; Aleman et al., 2005; Shuster and Lemieux, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: If inner speech is a special case of overt speech, then it would be expected to have an associated internal forward model.
source: If inner speech is indeed a special case of overt speech – 'a kind of action' – then it would also be expected to have an associated IFM (Tian and Poeppel, 2010 – see also Feinberg, 1978; Numminen and Curio, 1999; Whitford et al., 2012; Ford et al., 2001a).
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Inner speech does not elicit a measurable auditory-evoked potential.
source: A significant challenge in determining the existence (or otherwise) of an IFM to inner speech is that inner speech does not elicit a measurable auditory-evoked potential, which means that N1-suppression to inner speech cannot be determined directly using current methodologies.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current measurement techniques, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: The existence of an internal forward model to inner speech may be inferred based on how the production of inner speech suppresses the brain's electrophysiological response to overt speech.
source: However, the existence of an IFM may be inferred based on how the production of inner speech suppresses the brain's electrophysiological response to overt speech (Tian and Poeppel, 2010; Tian and Poeppel, 2015; Tian and Poeppel, 2013; Tian and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This statement describes an inferential approach and is supported by citations.

claim: The efference copy associated with overt speech is time-locked to the onset of the action.
source: A critical feature of the IFM associated with overt speech is that the efference copy is (a) time-locked to the onset of the action, and (b) contains specific predictions as to the expected sensory consequences of that action (i.e., is content-specific – Wolpert et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement describes a critical feature of the IFM and is supported by a citation.

claim: The efference copy associated with overt speech contains specific predictions as to the expected sensory consequences of that action.
source: A critical feature of the IFM associated with overt speech is that the efference copy is (a) time-locked to the onset of the action, and (b) contains specific predictions as to the expected sensory consequences of that action (i.e., is content-specific – Wolpert et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement describes a critical feature of the IFM and is supported by a citation.

claim: There was a significant main effect of Condition on the amplitude of the N1 peak in the inner speech experiment.
source: Repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of Condition (F(2,82) = 4.21, p = 0.018, ηp2 = 0.09) on the amplitude of the N1 peak.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: N1-amplitude in the Match condition was significantly smaller than in the Mismatch condition in the inner speech experiment.
source: Analysis of simple effects revealed that N1-amplitude in the Match condition was significantly smaller than both the Mismatch (t(41) = 2.54, p = 0.015, dz = 0.39, CI(95%) = [0.187, 1.649]) and Passive (t(41) = 2.77, p = 0.008, dz = 0.43, CI(95%) = [0.278, 1.776]) conditions (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 2c.

claim: N1-amplitude in the Match condition was significantly smaller than in the Passive condition in the inner speech experiment.
source: Analysis of simple effects revealed that N1-amplitude in the Match condition was significantly smaller than both the Mismatch (t(41) = 2.54, p = 0.015, dz = 0.39, CI(95%) = [0.187, 1.649]) and Passive (t(41) = 2.77, p = 0.008, dz = 0.43, CI(95%) = [0.278, 1.776]) conditions (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There was no difference in N1-amplitude between the Mismatch and Passive conditions in the inner speech experiment.
source: There was no difference in N1-amplitude between the Mismatch and Passive conditions (t(41) = 0.26, p = 0.800, dz = 0.04, CI(95%) = [−0.758, 0.977]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There was a main effect of Condition on the latency of the N1 peak in the inner speech experiment.
source: There was also a main effect of Condition on the latency of the N1 peak (F(2,82) = 5.03, p = 0.016, ηp2 = 0.11.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: The N1-peak occurred significantly earlier in the Match condition compared to the Passive condition in the inner speech experiment.
source: Analysis of the simple effects revealed that the N1-peak occurred significantly earlier in the Match condition compared to the Passive condition (t(41) = 3.15, p = 0.003, dz = 0.49, CI(95%) = [−6.927,–1.518]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference in N1-latency between the Mismatch and Passive conditions in the inner speech experiment.
source: There was no significant difference in N1-latency between the Mismatch and Passive conditions (t(41) = 1.76, p = 0.087, dz = 0.27, CI(95%) = [−6.298, 0.441]), nor between the Match and Mismatch conditions (t(41) = 1.29, p = 0.204, dz = 0.20, CI(95%) = [−3.316, 0.729]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference in N1-latency between the Match and Mismatch conditions in the inner speech experiment.
source: There was no significant difference in N1-latency between the Mismatch and Passive conditions (t(41) = 1.76, p = 0.087, dz = 0.27, CI(95%) = [−6.298, 0.441]), nor between the Match and Mismatch conditions (t(41) = 1.29, p = 0.204, dz = 0.20, CI(95%) = [−3.316, 0.729]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There was a main effect of Condition on P2 amplitude in the inner speech experiment.
source: One-way ANOVA revealed a main effect of Condition (F(2,82) = 6.60, p = 0.006, ηp2 = 0.14).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Amplitude of the P2 component was significantly smaller in the Mismatch condition relative to the Match condition in the inner speech experiment.
source: Analysis of the simple effects revealed that amplitude of the P2 component was significantly smaller in the Mismatch condition, relative to both the Match (t(41) = 3.54, p = 0.001, dz = 0.55, CI(95%) = [0.555, 2.028]) and Passive (t(41) = 3.21, p = 0.003, dz = 0.50, CI(95%) = [−3.549, –0.810]) conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Amplitude of the P2 component was significantly smaller in the Mismatch condition relative to the Passive condition in the inner speech experiment.
source: Analysis of the simple effects revealed that amplitude of the P2 component was significantly smaller in the Mismatch condition, relative to both the Match (t(41) = 3.54, p = 0.001, dz = 0.55, CI(95%) = [0.555, 2.028]) and Passive (t(41) = 3.21, p = 0.003, dz = 0.50, CI(95%) = [−3.549, –0.810]) conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The difference between the Match and Passive conditions for P2 amplitude was not significant in the inner speech experiment.
source: The difference between the Match and Passive conditions was not significant (t(41) = 1.26, p = 0.216, dz = 0.19, CI(95%) = [−0.540, 2.316]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There was a main effect of Condition on P3 amplitude in the inner speech experiment.
source: ANOVA revealed a main effect of Condition (F(2,82) = 5.86, p = 0.004, ηp2 = 0.13).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: The amplitude of the P3 component was significantly larger in the Match condition relative to the Mismatch condition in the inner speech experiment.
source: Analysis of the simple effects revealed that the amplitude of the P3 component was significantly larger in the Match condition relative to both the Mismatch (t(41) = 2.23, p = 0.032, dz = 0.34, CI(95%) = [0.117, 2.433]) and Passive (t(41) = 3.26, p = 0.002, dz = 0.50, CI(95%) = [0.813, 3.444]) conditions (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The amplitude of the P3 component was significantly larger in the Match condition relative to the Passive condition in the inner speech experiment.
source: Analysis of the simple effects revealed that the amplitude of the P3 component was significantly larger in the Match condition relative to both the Mismatch (t(41) = 2.23, p = 0.032, dz = 0.34, CI(95%) = [0.117, 2.433]) and Passive (t(41) = 3.26, p = 0.002, dz = 0.50, CI(95%) = [0.813, 3.444]) conditions (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 4c.

claim: There was no significant difference in P3 amplitude between the Passive and Mismatch conditions in the inner speech experiment.
source: There was no significant difference between the Passive and Mismatch conditions (t(41) = 1.31, p = 0.196, dz = 0.20, CI(95%) = [−0.458, 2.165]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: In the overt speech experiment, there was a significant main effect of Condition on the amplitude of the N1 peak for uncorrected data.
source: For the uncorrected data, repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of Condition (F(2,58) = 10.99, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.28) on the amplitude of the N1 peak.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: In the overt speech experiment, N1-amplitude in the Match condition was significantly smaller than the Mismatch condition for uncorrected data.
source: Critically, analysis of simple effects revealed that N1-amplitude in the Match condition was significantly smaller than the Mismatch condition (t(29) = 2.61, p = 0.014, dz = 0.48, CI(95%) = [0.472, 3.897]), consistent with the results of the inner speech experiment.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: In the overt speech experiment, N1-amplitude in the Passive condition was significantly smaller than both the Match and Mismatch conditions for uncorrected data.
source: However, contrary to the results of the inner speech experiment, N1-amplitude in the Passive condition was significantly smaller than both the Match (t(29) = 2.63, p = 0.013, dz = 0.48, CI(95%) = [0.646, 5.137]) and Mismatch (t(29) = 3.97, p < 0.001, dz = 0.72, CI(95%) = [2.461, 7.691]) conditions in the overt speech experiment (see Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In the overt speech experiment, there was a significant main effect of Condition on the amplitude of the N1 peak for motor-corrected data.
source: Repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of Condition (F(2,58) = 8.43, p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.23).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: In the overt speech experiment, N1-amplitude in the Match condition was significantly smaller than the Mismatch condition for motor-corrected data.
source: Analysis of simple effects revealed that N1-amplitude in the Match condition was significantly smaller than the Mismatch condition (t(29) = 2.46, p = 0.020, dz = 0.45, CI(95%) = [0.384, 4.190]), and that N1-amplitude in the Passive condition was significantly smaller than both the Match (t(29) = 2.20, p = 0.036, dz = 0.40, CI(95%) = [0.150, 4.243]) and Mismatch (t(29) = 3.43, p = 0.002, dz = 0.63, CI(95%) = [1.808, 7.159]) conditions (see Figure 5b, c and d).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 5b, c and d.

claim: In the overt speech experiment, N1-amplitude in the Passive condition was significantly smaller than both the Match and Mismatch conditions for motor-corrected data.
source: Analysis of simple effects revealed that N1-amplitude in the Match condition was significantly smaller than the Mismatch condition (t(29) = 2.46, p = 0.020, dz = 0.45, CI(95%) = [0.384, 4.190]), and that N1-amplitude in the Passive condition was significantly smaller than both the Match (t(29) = 2.20, p = 0.036, dz = 0.40, CI(95%) = [0.150, 4.243]) and Mismatch (t(29) = 3.43, p = 0.002, dz = 0.63, CI(95%) = [1.808, 7.159]) conditions (see Figure 5b, c and d).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 5b, c and d.

claim: Of the nine different phonemes tested, /BA/ and /BI/ were judged to be most similar in terms of their amplitude and overall shape.
source: Of the nine different phonemes, /BA/ and /BI/ were judged to be most similar in terms of their amplitude and overall shape, and hence these phonemes were chosen to be used as the audible phonemes in both the inner and overt speech experiments.
evidence: This is a judgment based on visual inspection of the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The production of inner speech resulted in sensory attenuation of the auditory-evoked potential elicited by a simultaneously-presented audible phoneme, in the absence of any overt motor action.
source: The present study used a novel experimental protocol to demonstrate that the production of an inner phoneme resulted in sensory attenuation of the auditory-evoked potential elicited by a simultaneously-presented audible phoneme, in the absence of any overt motor action.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: Sensory attenuation from inner speech was dependent on the content of the inner phoneme matching the content of the audible phoneme.
source: Crucially, the production of inner speech did not result in equal sensory attenuation to all sounds; sensory attenuation was dependent on the content of the inner phoneme matching the content of the audible phoneme.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: Inner speech production is associated with a time-locked and content-specific internal forward model, similar to the one believed to operate in the production of overt speech.
source: These results suggest that inner speech production is associated with a time-locked and content-specific internal forward model, similar to the one believed to operate in the production of overt speech (Hickok, 2012; Tourville and Guenther, 2011; Hickok and Poeppel, 2004; Houde et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Inner speech alone is able to elicit an efference copy and cause sensory attenuation of audible sounds.
source: In short, the results of this study suggest that inner speech alone is able to elicit an efference copy and cause sensory attenuation of audible sounds.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: There is strong evidence that the mechanistic basis of N1-suppression to overt speech involves an efference-copy mediated internal forward model.
source: There is strong evidence that the mechanistic basis of N1-suppression to overt speech involves an efference-copy mediated IFM (Eliades and Wang, 2003; Crapse and Sommer, 2008; Rauschecker and Scott, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A similar mechanism underlies sensory attenuation in the case of inner speech as in overt speech.
source: It thus seems reasonable to assume that a similar mechanism underlies sensory attenuation in the case of inner speech.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and prior knowledge.

claim: The idea that inner speech shares mechanistic features with overt speech is consistent with the conceptualization of inner speech 'as a kind of action'.
source: The idea that inner speech shares mechanistic features with overt speech is consistent with the conceptualization of inner speech 'as a kind of action' (Jones and Fernyhough, 2007, p.396) and, more generally, with Hughlings Jackson's belief that thinking is merely our most complex motor act: 'sensori-motor processes… form the anatomical strata of mental states' (Hughlings Jackson, 1958, p.49).
evidence: This statement connects the findings to prior theoretical work, supported by citations.

claim: Inner speech production resulted in N1-suppression if – and only if – the content of the inner phoneme matched the content of the audible phoneme.
source: It was notable that inner speech production resulted in N1-suppression if – and only if – the content of the inner phoneme matched the content of the audible phoneme; that is, only in the Match condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental finding.

claim: Differences in participants' attention or task-preparation may have contributed to the observed differences between the 'active' conditions and the passive condition.
source: Notwithstanding the fact that the N1-suppression effect has previously been found to be robust to variations in attention (Timm et al., 2013; Saupe et al., 2013) and trial structure (Baess et al., 2011), this nevertheless raises the possibility that differences in participants' attention or task-preparation may have contributed to the observed differences between the 'active' conditions and the passive condition.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential confounds, though it acknowledges prior evidence against this possibility.

claim: The observed difference in N1 amplitude between Match and Mismatch trials reflects the impact of participants' inner speech on their sensory response to the audible phoneme.
source: Consequently, we can conclude with confidence that the observed difference in N1 amplitude between Match and Mismatch trials reflects the impact of participants' inner speech on their sensory response to the audible phoneme.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and results.

claim: The contrast between Match and Mismatch trials demonstrates that inner speech, like overt speech, is associated with a precise, content-specific efference copy.
source: It is this contrast that demonstrates that inner speech, like overt speech, is associated with a precise, content-specific efference copy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The results of the inner speech experiment mirror those of previous studies which have found sensory attenuation to overt speech to be reduced or eliminated if auditory feedback deviates from what would normally be expected.
source: The results of the inner speech experiment mirror those of previous studies which have found sensory attenuation to overt speech to be reduced or eliminated if auditory feedback deviates from what would normally be expected; e.g., by pitch-shifting the feedback or providing foreign-language feedback (Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2006; Behroozmand and Larson, 2011; Behroozmand et al., 2011; Behroozmand et al., 2016; Larson and Robin, 2016).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: N1-amplitude elicited by an audible phoneme was significantly smaller when participants simultaneously produced the same phoneme in their overt speech (Match condition), compared to when they produced a different phoneme in their overt speech (Mismatch condition).
source: The key result from the overt speech experiment was that N1-amplitude elicited by an audible phoneme was significantly smaller when participants simultaneously produced the same phoneme in their overt speech (Match condition), compared to when they produced a different phoneme in their overt speech (Mismatch condition).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental finding from the overt speech experiment.

claim: The result from the overt speech experiment is consistent with numerous previous studies in the sensory attenuation literature.
source: This result, which is consistent with numerous previous studies in the sensory attenuation literature (Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2006; Behroozmand and Larson, 2011; Behroozmand et al., 2011; Behroozmand et al., 2016; Larson and Robin, 2016), was identical to the corresponding contrast in the inner speech experiment, in which participants had to produce phonemes in inner, as opposed to overt, speech.
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The auditory N1-component is sensitive to stimulus predictability, with predictable sounds evoking a smaller N1 than unpredictable sounds.
source: An alternative explanation for why N1 was smallest in the Passive condition is based on the idea that the auditory N1-component is (in addition to sound intensity, discussed previously) also sensitive to stimulus predictability, with predictable sounds evoking a smaller N1 than unpredictable sounds (Behroozmand and Larson, 2011; Bäss et al., 2008; Lange, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Both the inner speech and overt speech experiments showed the same basic pattern of results with respect to the key contrast: N1-magnitude was smaller if the phoneme generated by the participant matched the audible phoneme than if it mismatched.
source: In summary, both the inner speech and overt speech experiments showed the same basic pattern of results with respect to the key contrast: N1-magnitude was smaller if the phoneme generated by the participant (either covertly or overtly) matched the audible phoneme than if it mismatched.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from both experiments.

claim: Inner speech is associated with a precise, content-specific efference copy, as opposed to a generic and non-specific prediction.
source: These findings suggest that inner speech – like overt speech – is associated with a precise, content-specific efference copy, as opposed to a generic and non-specific prediction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The results provide support for the contention that inner speech is a special case of overt speech, which does not have an associated motor act.
source: Taken together, our results provide support for the contention that inner speech is a special case of overt speech, which does not have an associated motor act.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The notion that inner speech generates an internal forward model in the absence of an overt motor act has been hypothesized previously across several different literatures.
source: The notion that inner speech generates an IFM in the absence of an overt motor act has been hypothesized previously across several different literatures (Jones and Fernyhough, 2007; Feinberg, 1978; Scott, 2013; Guenther and Hickok, 2015; Ford et al., 2001b; Sams et al., 2005; Kauramäki et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: This hypothesis has been notoriously difficult to test empirically, due to the covert nature of inner speech.
source: However, this hypothesis has been notoriously difficult to test empirically, due to the covert nature of inner speech.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in the field, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Ford et al. found that sentences elicited a smaller N1-component when participants engaged in inner speech compared to when they did not.
source: Ford et al., (Ford and Mathalon, 2004) played participants repeated sentences over 30 s and asked them to reproduce the same sentences in inner speech. Ford et al., found that the sentences elicited a smaller N1-component when participants engaged in inner speech compared to when they did not, consistent with the results of the present study.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: Tian and Poeppel used MEG to show that the auditory cortex was activated immediately following production of an inner phoneme in the absence of auditory feedback.
source: More recently, Tian and Poeppel (Tian and Poeppel, 2010) used MEG to show that the auditory cortex was activated immediately following production of an inner phoneme in the absence of auditory feedback, which they took as evidence of an inner-speech-initiated efference copy.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: Tian and Poeppel found no difference in the amplitude of the M100 between the match and mismatch conditions in their 2013 study.
source: In a subsequent study, which was a strong influence on our own, Tian and Poeppel (Tian and Poeppel, 2013) asked participants to produce an inner phoneme within a 2.4 s window. This window was followed by an audible phoneme that could either match or mismatch the content of the inner phoneme. The authors found no difference in the amplitude of the M100 between the match and mismatch conditions, inconsistent with the results of the present study.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: Tian and Poeppel found evidence of M100 suppression to unshifted, undelayed audible phonemes relative to a passive baseline condition in their 2015 study.
source: Tian and Poeppel (Tian and Poeppel, 2015) asked participants to signal their production of an inner phoneme via a button-press, and measured the amplitude of the M100 component evoked by a pre-recorded audible phoneme of their own voice which matched the content of the inner phoneme, but which could be pitch-shifted or delayed. They found evidence of M100 suppression to unshifted, undelayed audible phonemes relative to a passive baseline condition, consistent with the results of the present study.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: Ylinen et al. found that audible syllables that were concordant with participants' inner speech elicited less MEG activity than discordant syllables.
source: Finally, Ylinen et al., (Ylinen et al., 2015) asked participants to mentally rehearse tri-syllabic pseudowords in inner speech. After several mental repetitions, an audible pseudoword was played which had either matching or mismatching beginnings and endings to the rehearsed pseudoword. The results revealed that audible syllables that were concordant with participants' inner speech elicited less MEG activity than discordant syllables, a result which is broadly consistent with the results of the present study.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: The experimental stimuli were physically identical across all conditions in the current experiment.
source: Firstly, the experimental stimuli (animation, audible phonemes, rating-scale, etc.) were physically identical across all conditions, as was the nature of participants' task (i.e., to fixate on the screen and produce an inner phoneme at a designated time).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The only thing that differed between the different trial-types was the inner phoneme that participants were asked to produce.
source: The only thing that differed between the different trial-types was the inner phoneme that participants were asked to produce.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The observed differences in sensory attenuation could not have been due to any physical differences between the conditions.
source: This meant that the observed differences in sensory attenuation could not have been due to any physical differences between the conditions (Luck, 2005).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design, supported by a citation.

claim: It was impossible to predict which of the two audible phonemes would be presented on any given trial.
source: Secondly, the fact that it was impossible to predict which of the two audible phonemes would be presented on any given trial meant that it was impossible to distinguish Match from Mismatch trials a priori.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The observed results could not have been due to between-condition differences in demand characteristics.
source: This meant that the observed results could not have been due to between-condition differences in, for example, demand characteristics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The 'ticker tape' feature of the current protocol enabled participants to very accurately time-lock the onset of their inner phoneme to match the onset of the external sound.
source: Thirdly, the 'ticker tape' feature of the current protocol enabled participants to very accurately time-lock the onset of their inner phoneme to match the onset of the external sound.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and its advantages.

claim: The position of the trigger line refreshed every 8.3 ms.
source: In the current protocol, the position of the trigger line refreshed every 8.3 ms, which presumably enabled participants to time the onset of their inner phoneme far more accurately than would be possible with a countdown sequence, mental rehearsal or open temporal window, such as have been used in previous studies (Tian and Poeppel, 2013; Ford et al., 2001b; Ylinen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, with inference about its advantages.

claim: The current protocol did not require participants to make an active movement to signal the onset of their inner phoneme.
source: Finally, the current protocol did not require participants to make an active movement to signal the onset of their inner phoneme, such as by pressing a button.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The present study provides arguably the strongest evidence to date that inner speech results in sensory attenuation of the N1-component of the auditory-evoked potential, even in the absence of an overt motor response.
source: In light of its methodological features, the present study provides arguably the strongest evidence to date that inner speech results in sensory attenuation of the N1-component of the auditory-evoked potential, even in the absence of an overt motor response.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the study's findings.

claim: The amplitude of the N1 component is volume dependent; loud sounds evoke N1-components of larger amplitude than do soft sounds.
source: The rationale for focusing on N1 lies in the fact that the amplitude of this component is volume dependent; that is, other things being equal, loud sounds evoke N1-components of larger amplitude than do soft sounds (Näätänen and Picton, 1987; Hegerl and Juckel, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The observation of N1-suppression in prior studies implies that the brain processes self-generated sounds as though they were physically softer than identical external sounds.
source: In prior studies of N1-suppression, participants have typically generated sounds through overt actions such as overt speech, button-presses etc. The observation of N1-suppression in such studies thus implies that the brain processes self-generated sounds as though they were physically softer than identical external sounds.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior research findings.

claim: The N1-suppression demonstrated in the present study suggests that the brain also processes imagined sounds as though they were physically softer than identical, unimagined sounds.
source: The N1-suppression demonstrated in the present study extends this idea by suggesting that the brain also processes imagined sounds as though they were physically softer than identical, unimagined sounds.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: This finding provides evidence that mental state influences perception at a fundamental level.
source: In addition to providing evidence that inner speech is associated with an IFM of similar nature to overt speech, this finding provides evidence that mental state influences perception at a fundamental level (Gregory, 1997).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Niziolek et al. found that the degree of sensory attenuation was stronger when participants produced vowel sounds that were closer to their median production of these sounds.
source: With regards to the question of what mechanism could underlie sensory attenuation to inner speech: a recent study by Niziolek, Nararajan and Houde (Niziolek et al., 2013) on sensory attenuation in the context of overt speech production found that the degree of sensory attenuation was stronger when participants produced vowel sounds that were closer (in terms of their acoustic properties) to their median production of these sounds, compared to when they produced vowel sounds that were, for them, less typical.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: The efference copy associated with overt speech production represents a sensory goal.
source: These results suggests that the efference copy associated with overt speech production represents a sensory goal (i.e., 'a prototypical production at the center of a vowel's formant distribution', p. 16115), and that the distance (in formant space) of any given utterance from this 'sensory prototype' determines its degree of sensory attenuation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: Filik and Barber provided evidence that people produce inner speech in the same regional accent as their overt speech.
source: In regards to the assumption that the sensory goals of inner speech are the same as overt speech, and that a person's inner voice is the same as their actual voice, there is some evidence in support of this conjecture: Filik and Barber (2011) provided evidence that people produce inner speech in the same regional accent as their overt speech.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: Other studies have reported evidence suggesting that inner speech has impoverished acoustic properties relative to overt speech.
source: However, other studies have reported evidence suggesting that inner speech has impoverished acoustic properties relative to overt speech (Oppenheim and Dell, 2008).
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: People with auditory-verbal hallucinations often report hearing multiple voices with different auditory properties.
source: It is also possible that inner speech can consist of several distinct 'voices', with each having specific auditory properties; the fact that people with auditory-verbal hallucinations often report hearing multiple voices with different auditory properties (McCarthy-Jones et al., 2014) is consistent with this idea, if – as discussed further below – auditory-verbal hallucinations ultimately reflect inner speech being misperceived as overt speech.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and involves speculation about the relationship to hallucinations.

claim: The N2 and P3 components are typically elicited by tasks in which the participant is asked to identify 'target' stimuli which are nested among 'non-target' stimuli.
source: The N2 and P3 components are among the most heavily investigated components in the ERP literature (Näätänen and Picton, 1986; Polich, 2007), and are typically elicited by tasks – such as the auditory oddball and Go/NoGo tasks – in which the participant is asked to identify (by means of a button-press, for example) 'target' stimuli which are nested among 'non-target' stimuli (Smith et al., 2010; Spencer et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The N2 and P3 can be elicited by tasks in which a mental response is required.
source: Critically, the N2 and P3 can also be elicited by tasks in which a mental response is required, such as when target stimuli have to be mentally counted as opposed to signaled with a button-press (Mertens and Polich, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Tian and Poeppel observed a larger M200 component in their match vs. mismatch comparison.
source: It is also worth noting that Tian and Poeppel (Tian and Poeppel, 2013) observed a larger M200 component in their match vs. mismatch comparison, consistent with the enhanced P2 observed in the Match vs. Mismatch comparison in the present study.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: The M200/P2 component may index something other than a sensory prediction, possibly involving a cognitive 'template matching' process.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the M200/P2 component may index something other than a sensory prediction, possibly involving a cognitive 'template matching' process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Some of the most characteristic symptoms of schizophrenia seem to reflect the patient misattributing, to external agents, self-generated motor actions and self-generated thoughts.
source: The implied existence of an efference copy to inner speech holds important implications for how to best understand some of the psychotic symptoms associated with schizophrenia. Some of the most characteristic of these symptoms seem to reflect the patient misattributing, to external agents, self-generated motor actions (e.g., delusions of control) and self-generated thoughts (e.g., delusions of thought insertion, auditory-verbal hallucinations – Feinberg, 1978; Frith, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: An influential account argues that psychotic symptoms in schizophrenia arise because of an abnormality in the internal forward model associated with both physical and mental actions.
source: An influential account of these experiences argues that they arise because of an abnormality in the IFM associated with both physical and mental actions (Feinberg, 1978; Frith, 1992).
evidence: This statement describes an influential theoretical account, supported by citations.

claim: This internal forward model abnormality leads to an inability to predict and suppress the consequences of self-generated actions, which leads to confusion as to their origins.
source: This IFM abnormality leads to an inability to predict and suppress the consequences of self-generated actions, which leads to confusion as to their origins.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical mechanism.

claim: The symptom of thought echo can be well explained as the patient's own inner speech being misattributed and misperceived as an external voice.
source: This hypothesis has a strong theoretical foundation: for example, the distinctive symptom of thought echo, in which the patient hears their own thoughts spoken out loud by an external voice, can be well explained as the patient's own inner speech being misattributed and misperceived as an external voice (Frith, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Numerous studies have provided empirical evidence showing that schizophrenia patients exhibit subnormal levels of sensory attenuation to their own physical actions.
source: However, while numerous studies have provided empirical evidence showing that schizophrenia patients exhibit subnormal levels of sensory attenuation to their own physical actions (Whitford et al., 2011; Blakemore et al., 2000b; Shergill et al., 2005), including subnormal levels of N1-suppression to overt speech (Ford et al., 2001a; Ford et al., 2007b; Ford et al., 2001c), there is little empirical evidence that schizophrenia patients show sensory attenuation deficits to self-generated mental actions such as inner speech.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Schizophrenia patients exhibit subnormal levels of N1-suppression to overt speech.
source: However, while numerous studies have provided empirical evidence showing that schizophrenia patients exhibit subnormal levels of sensory attenuation to their own physical actions (Whitford et al., 2011; Blakemore et al., 2000b; Shergill et al., 2005), including subnormal levels of N1-suppression to overt speech (Ford et al., 2001a; Ford et al., 2007b; Ford et al., 2001c), there is little empirical evidence that schizophrenia patients show sensory attenuation deficits to self-generated mental actions such as inner speech.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: There is little empirical evidence that schizophrenia patients show sensory attenuation deficits to self-generated mental actions such as inner speech.
source: However, while numerous studies have provided empirical evidence showing that schizophrenia patients exhibit subnormal levels of sensory attenuation to their own physical actions (Whitford et al., 2011; Blakemore et al., 2000b; Shergill et al., 2005), including subnormal levels of N1-suppression to overt speech (Ford et al., 2001a; Ford et al., 2007b; Ford et al., 2001c), there is little empirical evidence that schizophrenia patients show sensory attenuation deficits to self-generated mental actions such as inner speech.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: The failure to identify electrophysiological sensory attenuation deficits to inner speech in schizophrenia patients is not because the deficits do not exist, but rather because previous experimental protocols have been insufficiently sensitive to detect them.
source: We suggest that the failure to identify electrophysiological sensory attenuation deficits to inner speech in schizophrenia patients is not because the deficits do not exist, but rather because previous experimental protocols have been insufficiently sensitive to detect them.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the literature.

claim: Engaging in inner speech resulted in sensory attenuation of the electroencephalographic activity evoked by an audible phoneme, but only if the content of inner speech matched the content of the audible phoneme.
source: In conclusion, the present study demonstrated that engaging in inner speech resulted in sensory attenuation (specifically, N1-suppression) of the electroencephalographic activity evoked by an audible phoneme, but only if the content of inner speech matched the content of the audible phoneme.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: Inner speech evokes an efference-copy-mediated internal forward model, which is both content-specific and time-locked to the onset of inner speech.
source: These results suggest that inner speech evokes an efference-copy-mediated IFM, which is both content-specific and time-locked to the onset of inner speech, which is consistent with the existing literature on sensory attenuation to overt speech.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Inner speech may ultimately be 'a kind of action', and a special case of overt speech.
source: Cumulatively, this implies that inner speech may ultimately be 'a kind of action', and a special case of overt speech, as long suggested by prominent models of language.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: These findings provide an experimental framework for investigating sensory attenuation deficits in inner speech, such as have been proposed to underlie some psychotic symptoms in patients with schizophrenia.
source: Accordingly, these findings not only provide insight into the nature of inner speech, but also provide an experimental framework for investigating sensory attenuation deficits in inner speech, such as have been proposed to underlie some psychotic symptoms in patients with schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the study.
